meta.topic: SIT passes but production API fails

problem:
Crestline Bank has integrated a merchant payment API that lets a retail partner submit payment instructions and receive status updates. The integration passed system integration testing cleanly: every test case returned the expected response, the test merchant onboarded without incident, and the release was approved. On the first morning in production, a third of live payment submissions fail. Some return authentication errors, some time out, and a few return a success response while the downstream order record is never created. The retail partner's customers are waiting at checkouts, the partner's support team is escalating, and the bank's first instinct is to blame the code that passed testing a week earlier.

The investigation must resist that instinct. SIT and production differ in ways that are invisible in a test report: different endpoints, certificates, credentials, network routes, firewall rules, feature flags, rate limits, downstream versions and, above all, real production data. A test payload is clean and predictable; a live payload carries the full variety of real customers, addresses, characters and amounts. The learner must compare the two environments systematically, use production-safe telemetry to isolate the failing boundary, and decide what can be fixed safely without making the live problem worse. The case also tests judgement about rollback: fixing forward is tempting, but only after containment is assessed.
solution:
Start by containing the impact: stop new submissions if the failure rate is rising, tell the partner what is known and what is not, and confirm which payments have a financial effect and which do not. Then compare the environments side by side in a fixed order: endpoint and configuration, credentials and scopes, certificates and expiry dates, network routes and firewall rules, feature flags, downstream service versions, rate limits, and payload versions. Pull production-safe telemetry for failing requests: the correlation ID, the request and response at each boundary, timings, and the downstream outcome. Reproduce the failure in a controlled way with a production-like payload, never by replaying live customer payments blindly.

Separate the failure modes, because each has a different fix: authentication errors point at credentials, certificates or scopes; timeouts point at network, downstream latency or rate limits; success-without-order points at the response contract and callback or event delivery. For each mode, confirm the root cause with evidence, assess the rollback and containment options, and only then change the environment or the code, with a retest that uses the failing production shape. Record the environment differences in a parity checklist so the next release checks them before deployment, and add certificate expiry alerts, contract tests and synthetic monitoring so the failure is caught before customers see it.

decision.question: Crestline Bank's merchant payment API passed SIT but fails for a third of live submissions on the first production morning. Some fail with authentication errors, some time out, and some return success while no downstream order is created. You are the business analyst coordinating the investigation.

options.label: A
options.detail: Roll back production at once without investigation, since rollback always restores service.

options.label: B
options.detail: Ask the retail partner to resubmit all failed payments, since a retry will probably succeed.

options.label: C
options.detail: Conclude the code is faulty and start a code fix immediately, since SIT must have missed a defect.

options.label: D
options.detail: Compare configuration, identity, network, certificates, payload, dependency versions and production data across environments, using telemetry to isolate the failing boundary before changing anything.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because a SIT pass with a production failure points first at environment differences, not at code. Option C assumes a defect without evidence. Option B risks duplicate payments, since some submissions already returned success while the downstream record is missing. Option A may be right eventually, but rollback without knowing the cause can restore the same failure or lose in-flight work.

steps.title: Contain impact, notify partner and confirm which payments have financial effect
Collect failing correlation IDs and map each failure mode
Compare SIT and production configuration, endpoints and certificates
Check network routes, firewall rules, scopes and rate limits
Trace one success-without-order case across gateway, service, event bus and downstream
Apply the evidenced fix and retest with production-shaped payloads
Record parity checklist and monitoring actions in the release record

happy: Each failure mode is traced to a specific environment difference with evidence, the fix is applied and retested with production-shaped payloads, and the integration runs cleanly in production. The parity checklist, certificate alerts and contract tests are in place so the same class of failure is caught before the next release.

negative.title: Expired production certificate
negative.detail: The production certificate expired while the SIT certificate is still valid. Renew through the controlled process, verify the chain and expiry date, and add an expiry alert with an owner.

negative.title: Rate limit hit at live volume
negative.detail: Production traffic exceeds a downstream limit that SIT never approached. Confirm the limit with the provider, throttle or queue safely, and never silently drop payment submissions.

negative.title: Production-only data shape
negative.detail: A live payload carries a character, address format or amount that SIT data never included. Fix validation and mapping for the real shape, add the shape to contract tests, and hold affected payments for review rather than guessing.

negative.title: Success response but no downstream order
negative.detail: The API returns success on receipt while the event or callback that creates the order is lost. Treat HTTP success as receipt, not completion; trace the correlation ID, reconcile financial effects, and recover the order exactly once before any retry.

technical: Persist the idempotency key, payload hash, original payment reference, correlation ID and outcome for every submission, and keep SIT and production configuration as versioned, comparable records. Log the request and response at each integration boundary with the same correlation ID so a single trace shows where a payment stopped. Never log full credentials or secrets. Keep contract tests in the schema registry with consumer inventory, so a breaking change is caught before release, and record certificate expiry dates with owners and alerts.

accounting: A payment that returns success must be reconciled before any retry, because the debit may already exist even though the order record is missing. Hold ambiguous payments in a controlled recovery state and reconcile them against the ledger, the gateway log and the downstream order store using the correlation ID. Operations need a worklist of unreconciled submissions with ageing and service levels, and a rule that no operator replays a payment without checking its financial effect first. Certificate and secret expiry must be monitored as an operational control, not discovered by customers.

scenarios.then: the investigation tests configuration, identity, network, payload and dependency differences before code is blamed.

scenarios.given: an API returns success but the downstream record is absent,
scenarios.then: the same correlation ID is followed across each integration boundary and the failed transition is identified.

scenarios.given: a production-only payload shape causes failures,
scenarios.then: the shape is added to contract tests and affected payments are recovered exactly once.

questions.question: What should be checked first when SIT passes but production fails?
options: Environment differences such as configuration, certificates, network, flags and data
questions.explanation: SIT and production differ in configuration, identity, network, certificates, flags, limits and data, and those differences explain most SIT-pass and production-fail cases.

questions.question: What does an HTTP 200 or 202 response guarantee?
options: That the request was received or accepted at the transport level, not that downstream work completed
questions.explanation: HTTP success describes transport receipt or acceptance; business completion must be confirmed by status enquiry, events and reconciliation.

questions.question: Why is a blind retry dangerous after a success-without-order failure?
options: The debit may already exist, so a retry can duplicate the payment
questions.explanation: The payment may already have a financial effect even though the order record is missing, so reconciliation must come before any retry.

questions.question: Which control prevents the next expired-certificate outage?
options: Certificate expiry alerts with a named owner
questions.explanation: Expiry alerts with a named owner turn a silent calendar event into a managed operational control.
